newsitem.title: BELGIUM: KLM loses out in Lufthansa-VLM deal.
newsitem.headline: KLM loses out in Lufthansa-VLM deal.

text.p: Deutsche Lufthansa AG on Wednesday signed a cooperation deal with Belgian regional airline Vlaamse Luchtvaart Maatschappij (VLM), aimed primarily at increasing pressure on neighbouring Dutch rival KLM.

"The goal is to strengthen our competitive situation in Europe and here in this region of course especially against KLM," Lufthansa vice-president for network planning Harry Hohmeister told a news conference on the deal.
"From a strategic point of view, VLM complements our network in the low countries in an excellent way," he said.

VLM Chief Executive Officer Freddy Van Gaever said each year 60,000 to 70,000 passengers flew from Antwerp's Deurne airport, home to VLM, to London Gatwick or Amsterdam and from there connected to the worldwide networks of British Airways (BA) and KLM respectively.

"The Antwerp-Rotterdam-Munich link will be direct competition for those two existing lines," he said. VLM and Lufthansa will extend their cooperation from September with a new Antwerp-Rotterdam-Muenchen code-share route.
VLM, owned by Dutch entrepeneur Jaap Rosen Jacobsen, operates scheduled flights from the Antwerp, Rotterdam and Muenchengladbach airports to London City Airport.
From July flights from Rotterdam and Muenchengladbach to London City will be code-shared while VLM flights will also be integrated in Lufthansa's frequent flyer programme.
Hohmeister said Lufthansa had no immediate plans to purchase a stake of VLM. "We could perhaps discuss this in the future, but this should not be the first step," he said.
Van Gaever added VLM had been close to being bought by KLM but a full or partial sale was not being considered any more.
Homeister and Van Gaever declined to give financial details of the agreement "for competitive reasons".
VLM will continue to carry out passenger handling in Antwerp, Rotterdam, Muenchengladbach and London City while Lufthansa will do the handling in Munich, the company's second hub in Germany.
VLM, which has a code-sharing deal with Belgian Sabena for flights from Antwerp to London City Airport, has no plans for a similar deal with Air France.
"We cannot cooperate with everyone, Sabena and Lufthansa is more than enough," Van Gaever said.

He said the Lufthansa deal came in the wake of close takeover negotations with KLM last year which were eventually dropped by the Dutch airline which instead decided to challenge VLM through its Air UK partner on the same route.
"I still fail to understand such policy," Van Gaever said.
He said VLM had lost between 30 and 40 percent of its passengers to Air UK, but the number had been rising again in recent weeks.

Founded in May 1992 and operational from May 1993, VLM currently has seven Fokker 50 aircraft and has ordered two more. Three of the seven turboprop planes currently owned are leased to Spanish independent regional airline Air Nostrum.
Van Gaever said that the lease contracts had just been extended to the year 2001.
VLM expects to transport more than 200,000 passengers in 1997, compared with more than 150,000 in 1996.
Van Gaever said VLM made a loss in 1996, was likely to reach break even this year and was hoping for profit for 1998.
"Each year there is improvement. The alliances consolidate our future," he said.
